meta.title: Model Context Protocol
meta.thesis: Model Context Protocol is practical when learners can apply it to this concrete case: An IDE assistant needs a standard way to read docs, tickets, and repo state through approved connectors. By the end, they should be able to build or review MCP server contract for docs search and ticket lookup, measure tool-call success rate across clients, and catch the failure where each client invents a different connector shape and breaks permissions.

mentalMap.title: Model Context Protocol: mental map
mentalMap.caption: Teach MCP as host-neutral capability plumbing: hosts run clients, servers expose tools/resources/prompts, and policy stays with the host.
mentalMap.oneLineThesis: MCP standardizes how AI hosts discover and use external context; it is not an agent brain or a permission model.

modules.title: MCP is host-to-capability plumbing
modules.sub: It standardizes connection, not agent reasoning.
modules.summary: MCP gives capabilities a common protocol surface.
objectives: Define MCP host, client, and server.
Explain what MCP does not decide.
Choose MCP when reuse across hosts matters.

blocks.title: MCP is not the agent

spans.text: Problem anchor: a team wants the same KB search capability in a code editor, lesson studio, and internal chat. Without MCP, each host needs a custom adapter. With MCP, one server can expose search as a tool and notes as resources to compatible hosts.
The host still chooses the model, policy, UX, and approval. The MCP server exposes capabilities; it does not decide the plan or grant permission by itself.
If the same capability should work in more than one AI host, MCP deserves consideration.

blocks.analogy: MCP is a universal plug shape; the appliance still needs a power switch and circuit breaker.

blocks.title: Case study: shared course KB server

spans.text: The server exposes `search_lessons` as a tool, `kb://notes/{slug}` as a resource, and `draft_lesson_prompt` as a prompt template. A desktop host and web host can both connect through clients.
Each host applies its own auth, approval, and citation UI. The server does not become the product policy layer.

items.text: Identify the AI hosts that need the capability.
Define tools for actions, resources for context, prompts for templates.
Choose local stdio or remote HTTP transport.
Keep host-side policy around all calls.

blocks.title: MCP role

options.text: The client-server protocol for discovering and using tools, resources, and prompts.

blocks.explanation: MCP is integration plumbing, not autonomous governance.

modules.title: Handshake negotiates version and capabilities
modules.sub: Clients and servers initialize before useful work begins.
modules.summary: MCP starts with explicit lifecycle negotiation.
objectives: Explain transports at a practical level.

blocks.title: The lifecycle makes capability discovery explicit

spans.text: An MCP client opens a transport and sends `initialize` with protocol version and client capabilities. The server replies with its supported version, metadata, and capabilities. Only after `notifications/initialized` should normal listing and calls begin.
Transports matter operationally: stdio fits local desktop-style servers; streamable HTTP fits remote services with web hardening. Both carry JSON-RPC-style messages.
Pin and test the protocol version your host supports.

blocks.analogy: The handshake is a preflight checklist before the host uses the server.

blocks.title: Worked lifecycle for a local KB server

spans.text: The host launches a local stdio server. The client initializes, receives tools and resources capability metadata, then lists `search_kb` and `kb://lesson/{slug}` resource templates.
If the server writes logs to stdout instead of stderr, it can corrupt stdio protocol messages, so lifecycle tests should include startup noise.

items.text: Send initialize with version and capabilities.
Send initialized notification, then list tools/resources/prompts.

blocks.title: Lifecycle order
blocks.prompt: Why should a host wait for initialization before calling tools?

options.text: Because tools are always unavailable after initialization.
It needs compatible version and capability information from the server.

modules.title: Tools, resources, and prompts are different
modules.sub: Each primitive carries different UX and safety expectations.
modules.summary: MCP primitives encode intent: action, context, or template.
objectives: Use prompts for reusable task starters.

blocks.title: Primitive choice shapes host behavior

spans.text: Tools are callable operations and may have side effects. Resources are URI-addressed context that should preserve provenance. Prompts are reusable message templates selected by the user or host.
A KB article is usually a resource. A search operation is a tool. A “draft release note” workflow starter can be a prompt. Mixing them makes UX and policy harder.
Ask whether the model is acting, reading, or starting a workflow template.

blocks.analogy: Tools are buttons, resources are documents, prompts are forms.

options.name: Tool

cells.text: Search, create ticket, run query, mutate system.
Host approval and authorization still required.

options.whenToUse: Use when the model may request an operation.

cells.text: Can carry prompt injection; keep provenance.
Not higher priority than host policy.

blocks.title: Primitive fit
blocks.prompt: A KB note selected by URI should usually be exposed as what?
blocks.explanation: Resources are for readable context with provenance.

modules.title: Host policy wraps tool calls
modules.sub: MCP schemas validate shape, not permission or intent.
modules.summary: MCP is not a permission model.
objectives: Treat results and resources as untrusted content.

blocks.title: The host remains the safety boundary

spans.text: A server may describe `delete_file` with a perfect JSON schema. That only means arguments can be shaped correctly. The host still decides whether the current user, task, path, and approval state allow deletion.
MCP tool results and resources can contain hostile text. The host should label provenance, separate data from instructions, and avoid letting returned content override system policy.
If a server disappears or changes its tool list, the host should handle list-changed or call errors gracefully.

blocks.title: MCP-style host policy wrapper
blocks.explanation: The host checks tool existence, validates arguments, requires approval for external write risk, and preserves provenance on results.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Before reading the answer, predict whether `create_ticket` executes for an unapproved user.
predictThenReveal.answer: It does not execute. The wrapper returns a `needs_approval` status with the exact tool and arguments.

blocks.title: Policy layer
blocks.prompt: Why can’t an MCP input schema be treated as authorization?

options.text: It checks argument shape but not user permission, business policy, or approval state.

modules.title: Build servers with lifecycle hygiene
modules.sub: Protocol details become production reliability issues.
modules.summary: An MCP server is production software, not just a wrapper script.
objectives: Handle pagination, cancellation, progress, and errors.
Avoid stdout corruption for stdio servers.
Harden remote servers like web services.

spans.text: Server lists can change, operations can be long-running, and clients may cancel. Pagination, progress, cancellation, errors, ping, and list-changed notifications exist because hosts need predictable behavior.
Remote HTTP servers need TLS, auth, rate limits, tenant isolation, and token handling. Local stdio servers must keep protocol messages clean and send logs to stderr.
Test startup, list, call, cancellation, error, and shutdown paths before handing a server to agent workflows.

blocks.title: Verify AI output that used MCP

spans.text: Review both protocol and answer behavior.

items.text: The host connected to the expected server version and capabilities.
The primitive used was appropriate: tool, resource, or prompt.
Host policy approved or blocked tool calls before execution.
Returned content kept provenance and was treated as untrusted data.
Errors, cancellation, and tool-list changes produced safe user-visible behavior.

blocks.title: Server hygiene
blocks.prompt: Why should a stdio MCP server write logs to stderr?

options.text: Stderr is always hidden from developers.
Stdout is used for protocol messages, so logs can corrupt communication.
